summary: Introduces simple extensions to the Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL) so it can document routing policies for IPv6 and multicast address families.

eli5.summary: A common language for writing down who an Internet network is willing to share routes with, now updated for newer addresses.

questions: what is the afi attribute in rpsl
how to write ipv6 routing policy in rpsl
subtitle: How the language for writing down routing policy learned about IPv6 and multicast.

tldr.problem: RPSL could document routing policy only for IPv4 unicast, so networks could not describe their IPv6 or multicast policies in routing registries.
tldr.mechanism: RPSLng adds new mp- attributes with an optional address family identifier, a route6 class for IPv6 routes, and mp- variants on the set and router classes, while leaving the old IPv4 attributes untouched.
tldr.outcome: Existing tools and objects keep working, and IPv6 and multicast policy can be written in the same language. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 7909.

today: RFC 4012 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 7909. It in turn updated RFC 2622 and RFC 2725.

sections.title: Goals of the Extension
sections.content:
RFC 2622 defines the Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL) for IPv4 unicast routing, and RFC 2725 adds security extensions. RPSLng extends RPSL so that users can document routing policy for IPv6 and multicast.

The goals are to extend RPSL by address family, stay backward compatible with minimal impact on existing tools, stay clear because both people and software read RPSL, and avoid duplicating information when policies for different address families are the same. The result has to tell apart four policies: IPv4 unicast, IPv4 multicast, IPv6 unicast and IPv6 multicast.

This document updates RFC 2622 and RFC 2725.
sections.eli5: The old rulebook only had words for old-style addresses. This update adds words for new-style addresses without crossing out the old ones.

sections.title: Address Families and the mp- Attributes
sections.content:
In the aut-num class, policy is written with the import:, export: and default: attributes. Extending their syntax would break compatibility and muddy clarity, so these keep meaning IPv4 unicast policy. New multi-protocol attributes with the prefix mp- are added: mp-import, mp-export and mp-default.

Each takes an optional afi (address family identifier) list. If it is left out, the policy applies to all four families, the same as afi any. If one peering is covered by several attributes, the specification-order rule of RFC 2622 applies and the first matching specification is used.

The structured form of mp-import and mp-export supports EXCEPT and REFINE, and each exception or refinement may carry its own afi list. The RFC notes these are cascading, not truly nested, and that RFC 2622 wrongly called them nested.
sections.eli5: The old rule lines keep their old meaning. New rule lines start with mp- and can say which kind of address they are about, or all of them if you say nothing.

sections.title: Peerings, Filters and Examples
sections.content:
An <mp-peering> names an AS and optionally routers, using AND, OR and EXCEPT over AS numbers and AS sets, and over router addresses (IPv4 or IPv6), inet-rtr names and rtr-set names. EXCEPT is set subtraction, so (AS65001 OR AS65002) EXCEPT AS65002 equals AS65001.

An <mp-filter> is the RPSL filter extended so an address-prefix set can hold both IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes or prefix ranges. It is otherwise identical.

An address family set in an except or refine is valid only inside that expression. Constraints from the family can turn a filter into NOT ANY, for example an IPv4 prefix in an ipv6.unicast policy. Implementations may warn in that case.
sections.eli5: A peering says who you talk to, and a filter says which routes you accept from them. Now the filter list can mix old and new address styles.

sections.title: The route6 Class and Updated Classes
sections.content:
The route6 class is the IPv6 equivalent of route. Its class key is the route6 and origin attribute pair. Other attributes keep the same names but must hold IPv6 prefixes and addresses.

Existing classes get small additions. The as-set class needs no change; its evaluation is filtered by address family. route-set gains mp-members for IPv4 or IPv6 prefix ranges. filter-set gains mp-filter and peering-set gains mp-peering. A filter-set must have one of filter or mp-filter, and implementations should reject objects with both. A peering-set needs at least one of its two attributes.

The inet-rtr class gains interface, which covers IPv4 and IPv6 interfaces and tunnels (GRE or IPinIP), and mp-peer. The rtr-set class gains mp-members so it can list IPv6 addresses.

The dictionary also gets an ipv6_address type and a new protocol value, MPBGP, meaning BGP4 with multi-protocol extensions.
sections.eli5: Each kind of record in the registry gets a new field for the new addresses, and there is a new record type just for new-style routes.

sections.title: Authorization for route6 Objects
sections.content:
RFC 2725's authorization model is extended to IPv6. The mnt-routes and mnt-lower attributes apply to route6 and the new inet6num class, and mnt-routes may carry an optional list of prefix ranges in curly braces, or ANY. In aut-num objects, IPv6 and IPv4 ranges may be mixed.

To add a route6 object, the submission must satisfy two checks: the authentication on the aut-num object, and that on an applicable route6 object or, if none exists, an inet6num object. If the aut-num does not exist, the addition is rejected. The search looks for an exact prefix match, then the longest less-specific match.

In the chosen objects, mnt-routes maintainers are used if present, otherwise mnt-lower (only for a less specific inet6num), otherwise mnt-by. The submission must match an authorization in each of the two objects.
sections.eli5: Before someone can add a new route record, the registry checks that they are allowed to speak for both the network number and the address block.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says the extensions add no new security functionality or threats. It does remind readers that the original RPSL included weak authentication schemes: MAIL-FROM, which can be defeated by spoofing the source email address; CRYPT-PW, which is open to dictionary attacks and password sniffing if objects travel over unencrypted channels such as email; and NONE, which gives no protection.
sections.eli5: This update does not make the lock any weaker or stronger, but some old locks in the system were flimsy to begin with.
